content.title: About
content.content: Oatmeal is made from whole or processed oat grains, often served as a hot porridge. It is a popular fast‑food style breakfast that can be prepared in minutes by adding hot water or milk.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Oats are one of the oldest cultivated crops, grown for over 5,000 years.
Oat flakes are produced by steaming and rolling whole oat kernels.
Oatmeal is frequently used in vegan and gluten‑free recipes when certified gluten‑free oats are chosen.
In the United States, oatmeal is among the most consumed breakfast foods, especially in instant forms.
Oats contain beta‑glucan, a soluble fiber that helps lower cholesterol.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion, promotes satiety, and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains beta‑glucan
items.content: Beta‑glucan may reduce LDL cholesterol and support immune function.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Oatmeal provides thiamine, niacin, and vitamin B6, which are essential for energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: It supplies magnesium, iron, zinc, and phosphorus, important for bones, muscles, and nerves.

items.title: Low glycemic index when prepared properly
items.content: Oatmeal raises blood glucose slowly, which is beneficial for weight management and diabetes control.

items.title: Oat allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to oats or oat proteins.

items.title: Gluten cross‑contamination
items.content: Although oats are naturally gluten‑free, they are often contaminated with wheat during processing; those with celiac disease need certified gluten‑free oats.

items.title: High glycemic index in instant varieties
items.content: Quick‑cooking flakes can raise blood sugar faster than whole‑grain oats.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Prepare oatmeal by pouring hot water or milk over the flakes and letting it sit for 2–5 minutes. Add fruit, nuts, honey, spices (cinnamon, vanilla) or use it as a base for smoothies and protein bars.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store oat flakes in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For long‑term storage, keep them in the refrigerator to prevent the fats from becoming rancid.
